inline.s: Reply to Elder Wanshi

A good teacher’s dealings with people are like a lion training its cubs: in every crouch and every stretch it puts forth its full strength. Toward you, old as I am, I truly have grudged not a hair of my eyebrows. I rejoiced that you had entered the hall of Boshan and thought you would be wholly transformed, utterly shed. Yet the letter that has just come shows you still the same man as before. How sad! This shows how hard it is to enter the Way. If the metal will not submit to the forge and bellows, it will become an ill-omened ingot. Put forth your strength, sir. The trifles you require are not worth the eye of the Dharma; set them aside for now. Only press on at your own ground, and that is my hope.
To the Virtuous Prince of Shandong

I bow before Your Highness the virtuous prince: wisdom granted you by Heaven, good fruit planted in former lives, kindness melting within, benevolent grace shining without. Dwelling deep in the palace, you hold the mountains and forests in your thoughts; truly your roots in prajna are deep, and you are one whose merit and wisdom are both complete. This poor monk is a wild man beyond the clouds, yet again and again he has received your gracious regard, your tireless and earnest care. My heart flies to you over and over, my gratitude is very deep, and my shame has no place to stand. Yesterday I was fortunate enough to behold your majestic light and to trouble your noble person; we asked of the Way and spoke heart to heart, transcending dust and beyond the commonplace. This is truly a rare meeting of a thousand years, a blessing of three lives. Brief as a single breath it was, yet it surpassed many kalpas. And I was moved that your faith grows ever firmer, that you receive and accept without doubt, sentence striking sentence, heart dwelling in the Way. Moreover, you fear this limited birth-and-death, and take to heart impermanence, sickness and suffering. These are things the rich and noble do not keep in mind, yet the virtuous prince deliberately sets his will on them. Truly this stands far beyond the turbid world, and turns toward the gate of the Pure Land. Had you not planted roots of goodness over many lives, how could it be so? You have graciously asked about the practice of daily life; I respectfully set it out below.

Abstaining from killing can lengthen your years; lessening lust can ward off illness; stilling idle thoughts can make the true mind clear; cutting off afflictions can take you beyond the realms of suffering; Buddha-recitation can bring rebirth in the Pure Land; generosity and benevolence can govern a state; repentance can erase the obstacles of karma; compassion can nourish your ministers and people. Singing that fills the ear is not worth a thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name; a whole day of play is not worth a single day of quiet sitting. These are the highest merit, the wondrous method for warding off sickness, lengthening life, gaining many heirs and enduring blessing. The true mind is originally pure, but idle thoughts defile it, and so distress arises in turn. The Buddha’s body is originally one’s own mind, but ignorance screens it, and so its light does not appear. This very mind is Buddha; one’s own mind becomes Buddha. Reciting the Buddha is reciting the mind; contemplating the mind is contemplating the Buddha. When a single deluded thought arises, the Buddha becomes a living being. When a single hateful thought arises, the Buddha creates karma. When a single awakened thought arises, living beings become Buddhas. When a single kind thought arises, hell becomes heaven. Therefore it is said: the three realms are mind only, the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only. The mind makes heaven, the mind makes hell. When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; when the mind is defiled, the Buddha-land is defiled. Outside this mind not a shred of anything is to be had. So when the mind thinks defiled thoughts, one dreams at night of upside-down things; when the mind thinks pure thoughts, one dreams of wandering in fine scenes. Yet birth and death are like night and day, and all conditions are like a dream or an illusion, all transformed out of one’s own mind. If a person recites the Buddha with mind after mind and keeps the Pure Land in thought after thought, then the contemplation before him is accomplished, past karma is dissolved, the suffering of death does not entangle him, and at a single thought he is reborn in the Pure Land. Straightway he sees the Buddha, hears the Dharma, draws near Amitabha, and with the great bodhisattvas of the Land of Peace and Bliss roams the sea-gathering in the lotus pond. Hereafter, by the power of his compassionate vows, he will go to the ten directions to save living beings, no longer detained by birth and death, coming and going in the greatest freedom. This is the direct and swift Dharma-gate of practice; outside this mind, all else is deviant demons and deviant teachings. Hence it is said: there is only the short road of practice, so simply recite Amitabha Buddha. Never mistake the joy of the five desires in this turbid world, screening the originally pure true mind that is yours, and losing the originally pure Land of Bliss that is yours.
To the Prince of Shanyin in Puzhou

I remember how in former days, when I was begging my food among men and stood with my bowl at the gate of the great benefactor, you deigned to look on me with the eye of Dharma, forgetting rank and bending your dignity, so that this wild man, in his trivial way, quite forgot his own rusticity. Coming in and out of your vermilion doors, standing beside your jade countenance, I felt as though I roamed a thatched hut and dallied with gulls and herons. None but a man of understanding, one deeply certified to the unborn and forgetful of both self and things, could have let the fragrance of his virtue perfume another so that it unknowingly stained one’s heart and bones. Ten years since we parted, yet it seems but a moment. Even when I lived in cold places where the frost pierced to the marrow, at times some faint idle thought would stir in secret, and your wondrous voice and countenance would stand plainly in the mirror of my mind. Since entering Mount Tai, I have deeply relied on the filing and polishing of the wondrous master. Though I am ashamed before the ancients, I have at least not lost my first resolve, and I have some ground for confidence. I would not dare be untrue to a friend who knows me. After that the clouds scattered over Qingliang and the wondrous master betook himself to Luya, while I hid my form in the Eastern Sea; several more years have passed. Day by day I sit within the light of the ocean-seal, at peace in a calm and level world, where the dust-realms are still and body and mind draw daily farther away. Thus my tidings to the great benefactor have come at last to silence. It happened that the old monk of Wangu, following conditions on the sea, entered my pit, and asked after the Dharma-gate the great benefactor has certified, saying moreover that day by day he is deeper in the samadhi of illusion, that all existences are alike empty and his inch-wide mind dwells nowhere. I could not contain my joy. I have heard that men once thought lightly of a great jade disc and a team of horses, and thought much of advancing in this Way; and that there are those who skillfully enter the dust of toil and make it Buddha-work. I had not seen such a man; now I see him in the great benefactor. Truly you do not fail those of us who know you. Though mountains and rivers lie far and dim between us, the light of mind shines and illumines, not a hair’s breadth apart; the only fear is that when feeling arises we ourselves make the separation. Alas, this life is over, and there is no date for laughter and talk. I only pray that the great benefactor will set his mind at peace in one realm and look on death and life as equal; then we shall walk arm in arm in the field of stillness to the utmost bound, and who would compare this with those who merely share the same wind a thousand miles apart? I have not yet been able to bow at your feet, so I send this silent sound to knock at your dark stillness. I hope your spirit-pearl shines clearly; no need of many words.

I have not beheld your light; counting on my fingers, fifteen autumns have passed. Human life drifts by like a dream; is it really so? Only the wondrous accord that forgets words, where the true and the conventional are not two, endures. As for the way the benefactor stands toward me and my brothers, we are kin in Dharma, flesh and blood; between the two of us there is no third, and such a man is hard to find again. Whenever a single idle thought arises, the light of mind flashes out and the Dharma-body appears at once. From this I know that three thousand miles apart, not an inch of silk divides us; this is no empty saying. When the monk Longhua Tan arrived I received your Dharma words and read them three times over; one can see you have entered deeply into the sense of the inexhaustible. But this poor monk’s Zen is like the boxwood: an inch forward, a foot back. Not knowing my own measure, I let fall a word among men, and busybodies exposed it. I never thought it would travel so far to soil your heavenly eye; truly it adds to my shame. How dare I trouble you further for your seal of approval, and such excessive praise? If you grudge not your Dharma-affection, let it flow on without end, so that a thousand years hence men may glimpse a kindred spirit. Is that not more than mere voices answering one another? That the wondrous master carries the canon away to Jizu is truly one blow striking two places. But on a cloud-wandering of ten thousand miles, this heart cannot help hanging in suspense. There has been no word of Master Da; he is the lion of this age. He once spoke of wandering to gaze on the Three Qin and asked me to look in at his gate; I do not know whether he came. Yet this master’s style and bone are truly a sword across the sky: let a man come near, and the root of craving is severed forever. Is he merely able to make light of ten thousand households? I have often said that in the age of the semblance Dharma we might do without Linji and Deshan, but in the age of the final Dharma we cannot do without this old man.

For several years there has been no word between us; I suppose the great benefactor has stopped writing altogether. Human life is such a dream: should it not deepen one’s grief? The wondrous master built his seamless stupa and has already shown the model; surely it is kept in the benefactor’s secret treasury. If some day I come to borrow a look at it, I wonder how you would bring it out. I dwelt in the Naluo pit. My practice had no strength, and the mountain ghosts made sport of me, raising such an outcry that it shook the Thirty-Three Heavens and roused the wrath of the heavenly king, who cast me into the great bellows-furnace and forged me all over; body and mind were both melted away, bone and flesh wholly dissolved, until my house was broken and my people scattered. To this day I have been flung into the sea of miasma, a lone journey of ten thousand miles. Yet I rejoice that the fiery cangue has slipped off and that I walk on in gladness. I shall settle the unfinished public case of thirty years ago. I think when the benefactor hears of it, he will feel a pang in his heart. Now my hair has grown long and I am on the road; I fear the benefactor’s love does not cease, and that he will make of this a north-south separation, turning dreams upside down and disturbing his Zen joy. So I send this greeting: it is good news, not bad. I only pray that you and the wondrous master, with the light between your brows, illumine the ten thousand eight hundred lands. Yet this ten thousand miles lies still within your eyelashes; I do not know how you will gather me in.

The bygone matter of my dream was fully set out in my last letter. Since it was all upside-down, what more is there to say? Only this: in worldly appearances there is gain and loss, but in the Dharma-nature there is neither addition nor subtraction. One whose wisdom-eye shines clearly will surely not let it disturb his tranquil concentration. This wild monk has cast his illusory, empty body into the savage smoke and poisonous mists, as though sitting on a cliff a thousand feet high amid ten thousand years of ice and snow; even if a bone would not melt, it too is burned away. I wonder where the virtuous prince will look for Empty-Born in days to come. This wild monk is now in Wuyang and has received your Dharma decree; reading it, I perceive deeply how earnest your compassionate thought and concern are. Examining your various writings in detail, they all come forth from a refined mind and will surely shine for a thousand years. Recently, in the court gazette, I saw your memorial renouncing the world and the admonitory document; this is truly the bodhi-habit of the virtuous prince through kalpas, stirred and brought forth here, and it is also upheld by the power of the vow to bear the burden of living beings. I hold that if the virtuous prince can truly regard birth and death as a single hair, then he can surely draw a thousand catties with a single hair. With this, above for the altars of state, below for the common people, to bring his lord to the level of Yao and Shun, what difficulty would remain? Then he need not pass beyond the three realms to take up bodhi. But if the habit is stirred out of loyalty, and loyalty feeds the habit, he will not escape playing the madman; though he may win a high name, it will be hard to gather real fruit, and the worldly and world-transcending Dharma will both be lost. I think the virtuous prince must have found his own way to handle this. Then pray favor me with your instruction; I crane my neck for your virtuous word to comfort this anxious longing of mine.

From the northern frontier to the southern sky we hang ten thousand miles apart. In the perfect vision of the wisdom-eye there has never been any interval; it is deluded feeling that blinds itself. How could there be no thought of coming and going? I wonder whether the benefactor has lately been taking his joy in the Dharma, and whether he can be free of decline and affliction. I have heard that the Buddha, for the sake of King Prasenajit, pointed out the vision that does not shift and sealed it with the sight of the river. Do you, virtuous prince, standing all day by the stream, see the passing water as it is and yet see that which has never gone? Formerly I used to hear men say that the four elements are impermanent while the Buddha-nature is truly constant, and I took this for a secret seal. Now I say it is not so. Why? Because the Dharma-nature is everywhere present even in the insentient, and every dharma is real; then the five aggregates are originally empty, and what loss could the four elements add? Beholding the light of the Buddha’s adamantine relics, one steeps a body with outflows in a thought that is unborn, and thereby makes the Buddha-nature that is permanent and indestructible. Compared with beholding the whole body of the Sixth Patriarch, truly the Buddha’s word was no idle saying. Do you, virtuous prince, look on this illusory body as a moon in water, an image in a mirror? If in this you seek it and cannot find it, then turning back to what lies before you, you will say all is illusion and transformation, and the feelings of grief and worry will have nowhere to lodge. With my dull faculties I had not entered this forge and bellows, and could not escape falling into the view of half-arising, half-ceasing. Now that I have entered the ocean of the Lankavatara’s Dharma-nature, I see clearly through the knowledge and views of former days, and they are no more than a fish-eye’s false pearl. Hence I know that the ancients would not lightly approve a man; they had to reach the place where the source is exhausted and the tracks are cut off. This is hardly to overpower others with knowledge and views; still less is it a matter of holding fast or letting go, for all such is idle talk. When one sees how Yongjia met the Sixth Patriarch, all fox-doubts melt away at once like ice. How would the virtuous prince’s wisdom-illumination judge this? The Notes on the Lankavatara are all this dull-rooted monk’s public cases of repentance over the years. I send them to the virtuous prince to judge together with the wondrous master. If in them there is room for a needle to stand, then this dull-rooted monk should be banished to the Iron Enclosure.

Counting, it is nearly thirty years since I parted from the old benefactor; a mere instant. Truly thought and kalpa are one and the same time. I only fear that in this floating world a human life holds but a few phantom shadows, and that good friends and excellent conditions cannot be met again. Moreover, our paths lie in different directions, as though we were separated by a whole age. Even if our spirits understand each other clearly, our forms and traces cannot follow; to speak of it makes one grieve. Formerly Dayi came from Hezhong bearing your Dharma decree, and now in a flash another three years have gone. So does the sun and moon cheat a man. Your letter tells me that your Dharma-body endures age well and your bones and sinews grow stronger still. This old benefactor has been perfumed by prajna through many kalpas and took the adamantine seed as his embryo; moreover, being one who acts as true lord to what is carried along by the maker of things, how could he not be strong? This comforts me deeply. This wild monk’s illusory body has entered the forge; thanks to Heaven’s grace molding and smelting it, the dregs are gradually seen to settle away. I stroke my heart in gratitude and shame, having no way to repay. Though I sit in a land of miasma, I do not dare for a single thought forget my lord’s grace and the Buddha’s kindness.

A man in this world is suddenly like a traveler far from home. How much more so when, with a remaining breath of life, one holds a frail drifting body and is a guest within a guest, in this blazing wilderness and sea of miasma where poisonous vapors reek. I know the virtuous prince thinks of me thus, and does not know that I think of the virtuous prince thus. Since entering this land of guilt I have received your Dharma voice three times; it rings clearly in my ears. Recalling our old roamings, not a hair’s breadth divides us: so I know that the ancients’ meaning of non-shifting lies exactly in one’s own daily use. In recent years the taste of Dharma here has been no shallow thing, only I cannot share it with one who knows me. Yesterday a certain man came, and I learned fully of the virtuous prince’s daily life. I understand that the eldest prince is perfectly kind and filial; this comes from the bodhi-seed in his nature, and now that he has entered the holy womb and gained the power of nurture and growth, why fear that he will not reach its wonder? I am also glad that you sustain your aspiration by poverty and nourish your wisdom by tranquility; this too comes from the power of vow. In the blazing burning house, to seek a cool and refreshing man such as this: how rarely seen! Only the virtuous prince, roaming illusorily in this floating world, finds nothing that contents his heart; what contents it is just this mild and plain flavor. The wondrous master’s seamless stupa: he held out its model with one hand, and it is there at the corner of the virtuous prince’s head-wrap; even now it seems to well up from the earth. But I do not know whether the host of emanation bodies has assembled, nor who will snap his fingers to open the door of the jeweled stupa, gathering gods and men, so that all may see the whole body of Many-Treasures. Nor do I know whether living beings in the dark places can see this whole stretch of radiance.
To Zeng Jianzhai, Chief of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices

You alone, sir, have deep and sincere faith and a true heart set on the Way; you are not to be compared with those who go by voice and appearance. As for carrying out the two benefits in secret, harboring the mind that guards the Dharma, and taking this Way as your own charge, of such men as you and two or three gentlemen there is no lack. What fortune for the final Dharma, what fortune indeed! In my private thought, to be a master amid the dust is the hardest thing to find in a man, since he stands in the deep pit of the five turbidities and their afflictions. To set out for home along the very road one is on, and to certify bodhi without leaving one’s present place: none but a bold and vigorous man would dare look to it. If one truly takes birth and death as the great matter, the first requirement is to possess the adamantine right eye, to see through the various illusions before one and not be led astray by the jugglers of the five desires, not be screened by right and wrong, self and others, not be confounded by rank and wealth, not be shrouded by body, mind and world, not be entangled by idle thoughts of hate and love. Then one dwells in the world as in space, lives in the dust unstained, and may be called one who skillfully enters the unimpeded gate of great liberation. This is why, when Ananda showed his drowning, the World-Honored One pointed him only to the samadhi of illusion; it was precisely for this. Since you, sir, take the matter of birth and death urgently to heart, I pray you try entering this samadhi. If you enter it truly, then it is like a great mass of fire: wherever it touches, all is transparent; what thing would dare come near it? Worldly men who study the Way all abandon what lies before them and seek the mysterious elsewhere, not knowing that the wonder lies right before them; thus they mostly make obstacles for themselves and gain no true benefit. And they breed measureless opinions besides, talking sideways and up and down, never knowing that it lies exactly within seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing; one need only see through the false and not be deceived by it. The Buddhas and patriarchs teach the Dharma as a riddle-monger does, holding out only an empty fist to men. The deluded do not know this, and think there really is something extraordinary there, breeding measureless calculations. The wise man sees through it and only laughs. Seen thus, the Buddhas and patriarchs too have nothing extraordinary; they are simply men not seduced by illusions. Hence it is said: in the great theater of players, one is noble and then one is base; the mind knows they are the same, and therefore feels neither delight nor disgust. Seeing through, there is no delight or disgust; with no delight or disgust there is no grasping; with no grasping there is no obstruction; with no obstruction one attains liberation; having attained liberation there is no dharma and no bond; with no dharma and no bond, one is no longer detained by birth and death. Such a one may be called a man of great wisdom with the adamantine eye. To certify the truly constant without leaving birth and death, to ascend the Buddha-ground without treading a path: is he not a bold and mighty man? I remember how in former days a single phrase of the unimpeded gate of great liberation happened to leap out before you, and you set your mind to probe it. I often raised its jade ring, watching the movement and stillness of your eyes; it seemed you had not yet shouldered it with your whole body. So though I went more than a hundred cities away, the mind of Dharma-affection would not settle. I grudge not stretching out a hand from afar to raise it for you once more, and hardly notice that my tongue drags on the ground.

Thinking afar of our true bond in the Way, it transcends form at once and wonderfully accords beyond words; from the first there is no self or other. Yet because I live alone in the deep and dim, my loneliness is deep and my heart is still; how could I not lean on the flesh and blood within the Dharma? A while ago the pure one Yuezhi came, and I learned that your movements and repose surpass the ordinary and that you are good at the practice of daily life, growing ever more subtle and close. Adverse and favorable conditions alike are nothing but Buddha-work. I only fear that within Buddha-work you may add to knowledge and views, and make of it a thorn of illness. Looking into it, this matter is originally one true and equal ground, functioning spontaneously before you, utterly without obstruction. The reason we do not gain true benefit is precisely what is called the four marks secretly working the spirit, while one does not feel one is resisting. Alas for the final Dharma: the five desires burn fiercely and all are scorched. Who is willing to set his heart on a cold place? You alone bear it up with strength. Had your roots in prajna not been deep, how could your faith be so firm? I further hope you will strive in accord with the times, with your will set on the other shore, so as not to fail the hopes of one who knows you in the Dharma. Nayan lies in a far eastern backwater and has long been buried and turned upside down by the hosts of barbarians. Not measuring myself, I have happened to stand in its path. I dare not claim to raise up a famous mountain, but I do wish to save the hard-to-save. Were it not that within I rely on this inch-wide mind and without I am upheld by the spiritual power of the great teachers, I would not dare leave even my shadow in a stone chamber.

In the tenth month I received your Dharma voice coming from the west; it was as though your countenance stood before my stone chamber. Not only did it show the purity of your remembrance, it also showed how rich your mind of the Way has grown, and clearly revealed your lofty embrace. How could I not leap with joy? Alas, the world’s way is in decay and men’s minds are drowned, rushing on like fire and never turning back; none seems to know what is his own. How can the great matter of birth and death be worth a word to them? Only you, sir, say that this matter is the greatest, and take it so bitterly to heart; this is truly what a bold and vigorous man can do. But I do not know whether in the daily round of favorable and adverse conditions you can see through them, and whether you can wear away all afflictions and habitual tendencies. This matter I set my will on earnestly in early years and thought it something ten thousand times extraordinary; only in these fifteen years, having passed through ice and snow and looked at it from a cold place, I find it has no peculiarity at all. I pray you only take this body, mind and world, and with one thought of perfect observation see through them, as images in a mirror: coming, nothing clings; going, no trace remains. Let this wisdom stand before you like a great blazing furnace; then all conditions, afflictions, habitual tendencies and idle thoughts will touch it as a flake of snow or a thin frost, unable to stay near, and it will be like Tai’e sword held up in the sky: who would dare cross its edge? Such a one is called a man of great freedom. Why so? Because our original substance is the wondrous clear true mind, perfectly illumining the Dharma-realm, and originally without the marks of body, mind, self, others, world, birth and death. From the first deluded stirring of a single thought there is birth, and because of birth there is extinction. Since there is birth and extinction, it is called birth and death; since there is birth and death, the false marks of body, mind and world appear complete, and one is shrouded by them. This is what is meant by deluding the originally perfect clarity and so producing the false. Thereupon we take it for real and cannot see through it; therefore we are detained by birth and death, and in every circumstance, whether rank and wealth, self and others, right and wrong, joy, anger, sorrow and delight, idle thoughts and feelings, children and kin, all manner of attitudes and all karma of birth and death, are present before us, and thought after thought we wrestle with them. How could a single thought rest for a moment? If one thought cannot even rest, how could one perfectly observe and see through, so that they are extinguished on the spot like a flake of snow in a red furnace? Thus, though one takes birth and death to heart, one does not know the root of birth and death. Because one cannot see through it there, and because the will to seek the Way stands opposed to it, one breeds measureless thoughts of delight and disgust, of calculation and scheming. The deeper the scheming, the more urgent the revulsion, the heavier the distress; one thinks one must first abandon everything before one can succeed, and if one cannot in this life, then one is cut off from it for this whole life. Is that not to live in vain and die for nothing? This is the common failing of men of aspiration in the world. As for those who have the will to work at practice amid the dust of toil and conditions, they take the clear and numinous awareness of seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing, and the thoughts that arise and cease in dependence on dust and conditions, as real, and say that this very thing is it; this again is an illness within an illness, the hardest of all to cure. For even if one extinguishes all seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing and guards the still and idle within, that is still a shadow of discrimination among dharmas; this is precisely what is called the shadowy brightness of the consciousness-spirit, the mechanism of idle thought, the burrow of birth and death, the great obstacle of the knowable. If this is not yet real, how much less those restless things that depend on dust. Because they have no one of true knowledge and insight to decide for them, most drift into this fault, seeing unclearly and not seeing through. Then though they take up birth and death, they truly add to birth and death; is that not an illness within an illness? Since you, sir, take birth and death bitterly to heart, I pray you do not sit down inside this, nor scheme and weary and wait for the future; only in your daily practice take all conditions, afflictions, body, mind and world and see through them one by one, so that not a single dharma remains before you to face you plainly. Before a single idle thought is born, fix your gaze on it once and for all; let all manner of transformations arise and cease as they will, but never follow after them. It is like a bright mirror on its stand: though forms appear, there is no trace of coming or going. Gazing thus, in time it becomes perfect and clear of itself. With perfect clarity, arising and ceasing have nowhere to lodge; with arising and ceasing lodging nowhere, where could birth and death lodge? This, though not the essential wonder, is the crucial first step of a beginner. You look on me through the Way, and so we are flesh and blood within the Way; since you take birth and death bitterly to heart, you should set to work wherever you are, and not scheme and wait and throw away the days and months for nothing. My words run on as they come and I do not know how to cut them; I pray you illumine them clearly and strive with all your strength.
To Wang Nanming, Director of the Imperial Stud

I remember how in former days I waited on you, elder, in the city of Vaisali, and you deigned to illumine me with your compassionate light. Not disdaining me for my inferiority, you conferred on me the adamantine samadhi of illusion. At that time I still dwelt among sounds, forms and appearances; though I grasped it in mind and met it in spirit, my eye was still dull and my head still muddled. As for the vast, free, unimpeded gate of liberation, I was deeply convinced that none but you, elder, had certified it, and that no one else had entered it. I knew it indeed, but could not attain it. You showed me the Dharma, moved me by concentration, pulled me up by wisdom, laboring for me again and again, wishing you could make me shut the gate for seven days and leap in at one bound. Dull as I was, how could I not have leapt up with courage? But because not a hair had penetrated, it was like a thousand mountains between us; this is the true and earnest word of the ancients who personally certified and truly arrived. Afterward you, elder, hid yourself in the body of an official and departed, and further taught me to serve well my good friend Chan Master Miaofeng. You had no other thought, elder; you grieved that the Dharma-gate lay desolate and looked to this trifling one to carry the burden. At parting you lingered, spoke a verse in earnest admonition, sincere beyond the words, no less than flesh and blood. How could that be ordinary feeling? It was all Dharma-love. When the shares of Qingliang were distributed, I staked my life to serve a teacher; toward such a master as Miaofeng I had no second intent. Therefore ten years in rocky caves, a lone brightness burning steadily; a single thought of ice and frost, mind after mind illumined alone. Though it pierced me to the marrow and I was ashamed before the ancients, as for the many small resting places, I had some confidence. All of this flowed out from the great light of your wisdom, elder. Dare I forget its source and be untrue to one who knows me? Lately I have learned that you, elder, have deeply certified the unborn and play in the human world. I had wished to shake my staff once and walk three times around your meditation couch to thank your compassionate kindness, but past karma drew me away to the Eastern Sea. I love these deep mountains and great marshes, and my will is to take in these dry bones here and rest. As for your wondrous voice and countenance, elder, they have never left my samadhi. Would the old man of the Man Chamber fail to stretch out his right hand from afar, across the city of abundance, to stroke my head once and gather me in?
To Zhou Youhai (Tianqiu)

Formerly I followed you, elder, roaming in the city of the kings, and once sat in a high tower at the crossroads talking with you of non-duality. Since then, in the blink of an eye, ten years have passed, and all has become the Dharma-gate of a dream. I dwelt on Mount Wutai for seventeen years, until the cold pierced heart and bone and this illusory body could not bear it; so I sought far away the Yang Valley of the Eastern Sea and built a hut to live in. The place I dwell in has two strongholds; this famous site of the Eastern Sea is none other than the old Nala-yana pit recorded in the Buddhist scriptures. I chose the deepest and most secluded spot, whose form backs onto a host of mountains and faces out to swallow the grey sea; peaks embrace it all around and a hermitage is hidden within, a natural wonder. I built several bays of a meditation hall, just to dress the work of the maker of things and to shelter this illusory assembly. Above it leans on the highest heaven, below it looks down on the boundless; it is exactly like a mirage congealed, with long waves entering the seats and fish and dragons circling the steps, while the company of Brahma-walkers pace up and down, their shadows sinking in the empty water, entering straight into a mirror of lapis lazuli. I think to myself that you, elder, are advanced in years and sadly lack the gear to master such a view, and so it seems you cannot enter this ocean-seal samadhi. I venture to ask for several fine pieces of your writing to hang in the high pavilion, and then several long inscriptions besides, to vie in beauty with heaven and earth; then your Dharma-body, elder, will forever dwell herein. Can you, elder, grant this wish?
To Qu Taixu

In former days I carried a single bowl and walked to the city of the kings, and first waited on you, elder. Again you deigned to illumine me with your wisdom-eye, and I entered at once the gate of non-duality. We joined our couches and drew up knee to knee, and often talked through the whole night, causing all the newly resolved bodhisattvas to bring forth the supreme bodhi. This one excellent bond of prajna was upheld by your past vows, elder. I sigh that in this final Dharma the Way has grown so thin; seeking its true meaning, all who remain among forms and appearances seem men of a bygone age, and I never fail to slap my thigh in deep mourning. As for dispelling the fog of doubt in the heaven of the nature, and seeking the dark pearl in the sea of wisdom, who but you, elder, with the hand of the image-seeker, could undertake it? At our farewell in the western suburbs the snow filled the Jetavana grove; a single phrase revealed the heart and pierced to the marrow, so that heavenly flowers fell in confusion, Indra and Brahma bowed in reverence, the sun of wisdom shone perfect and clear, and the demon palaces shook and split. This bond too is no shallow one. After parting, though three thousand miles apart, not a step has moved; through a million Dharma-gates this inch-wide mind dwells nowhere. Following conditions along the road, I reached Baixia only on the summer solstice. All has gone well. On the day appointed for carrying the great canon into the monastery, the relics scattered through the highest heaven and auspicious light appeared above the stupa; light upon light faced north, net upon net interlaced, and the tile and rubble and dense thickets were all golden. Gods and men gazed up in countless numbers. The signs of response reached such a pitch as this. Was it not the latter half of a verse from you, elder, foretelling it in advance? Within a month the work was done, and I returned to the sea. By the twenty-fifth, before the year’s end, I had already entered the pit, and together with the host of dragon-elephants I recited your inexhaustible meaning, elder, and each and every one brought forth the mind of perfect enlightenment. I only wonder whether the great bodhisattvas in Vimalakirti’s chamber can be free of weariness in body and mind.
To Gu Langzai

Since we parted I have sat in this land of miasma, dining on mountain mist and drinking poisonous fog; the taste is much the same as gnawing snow and swallowing felt. Often I think of the dragon-flower tree, of talking softly heart to heart, of the light of the ocean-seal and long chanting and whistling. This scene, this hour: at a single stirring of memory the blazing heat vanishes at once. So again it is you who wash this heart of mine. This is something not even a dream could reach. The burning house of Chang’an is no less than the burning south; who will cool your fever of vexation for you? This wild monk’s heart and guts of ice and snow, of which the use is inexhaustible, all lie in the several new carvings; I would share them with you.
A Word of Thanks to Mao Wenyuan, Censor

At first I thought how few walk the world’s Way, and knowing myself to be a useless gourd, I was content to hide in rocky caves. Then I saw how in this remnant of the final Dharma men’s hearts are not as of old, and that for the most part they invert skin-deep gain and loss; so I fled to the sea to rest myself. I never expected that the sage’s grace is without partiality and the Dharma-cloud spreads wide, its light covering the whole land and overflowing even onto the thatched and grassy. You have sent down this grand bestowal and set this famous mountain here to endure for ten thousand generations. Yet though it is a by-work of right governance, it is truly what is meant by one who would govern the world taking it as the work of true governance. Since receiving the charge, I have trembled day and night; the man is small and the matter heavy, and I cannot spread the teaching abroad. I truly fear I may fail the sage’s heart and bury the sage’s canon; this fear pierces heart and bone. Lately Heaven has favored us with Your Excellency, who manifests the body of an official and does Buddha-work; in the snap of a finger you have made the ocean-seal shine forth, made Mount Sumeru heave, made gods and men rejoice, and shattered the demons of illusion, so that the true command of the Dharma-king is fully displayed and living beings turn toward transformation. Is this not because you wondrously accord with Vulture Peak, and moreover ride the power of past vows, meeting the occasion in form and shape, and blow the reed-pipe of this Way? Truly it may be called the worldly and the world-transcending Dharma meeting and returning together, the true and the conventional both restored, with men and non-men rejoicing beyond measure. I respectfully hold that the merit of this prosperous age is as high and deep as the mountains and seas, and that Your Excellency’s Dharma-body shall be as enduring as the altars of state. As for the work of building, I have received the Dharma decree that I alone am to take it as my whole charge; this truly saves trouble and expense, and is especially convenient for the authorities. But the monastery lies deep in the mountains with the roads cut off, and in all things needed and used there is no little difficulty. Fortunately Ma Jimo has put his strength to maintaining it. In this remote border place there is no one to write or carve, and much of it is not as it should be; only three steles are finished, and one postface remains, which I shall take up in turn. The timber is in the south and has not yet arrived; the weather is turning cold, and the stele pavilion must wait for the thaw of spring to be built. For now I send this report, to settle the public case before me. This excellent bond is not easily come by; I beg Your Excellency to join with the Grand Censor in each letting fall a single turning word, by way of Dharma-giving. Then not only will the mountain spirit be doubly honored, but ten thousand generations hence men will still glimpse your wondrous voice and countenance among these lone peaks and scattered rocks. I have scribbled this rudely before your dignity, and am overcome with trepidation.
To Zhang Shouan

I have heard the Buddha say that a bodhisattva who studies prajna thereby shoulders the Tathagata. Now I see you, sir, applying your mind thus and seeking the supreme bodhi; truly the World-Honored One’s word was no idle saying. I take to heart that in the final Dharma the gates of Dharma decline; had you, sir, not shouldered it with your whole body, how could the compassionate Honored One’s light illumine the ten directions? And take the gods, who mostly enjoy the pleasures of desire and do not rouse the bodhi-mind: without you, sir, sounding the heavenly drum and teaching without deliberation, how could they understand the Buddha’s wisdom? Thus you are one who truly repays the Buddha’s kindness; but who is there to repay your kindness? I recall the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who gave to every person the prediction of buddhahood, and who bore with patience even curses and blows. This is because our Buddha saw that living beings in this final Dharma are mostly hard and unyielding, hard to transform; if a bodhisattva vows at such a time to spread the Buddha-Dharma, he must possess the power of firm patience, the power of diligence, and the power of great compassion, and only then can he skillfully enter the dust of toil and do Buddha-work. If these three powers are not full, and a single thought of retreat arises, he cannot leap beyond the five turbidities at once. This poor monk reckons that the World-Honored One has appeared in the east and sits at ease in the ocean-seal practice-ground, reciting the Avatamsaka day by day without a break through the six periods, and moreover teaching skillfully, expounding all dharmas by way of parables and causes; at once he makes dragons and gods rejoice and stubborn stones nod, and the ten directions gather like clouds, so that the bodhisattvas cannot push them apart. Yet in Vimalakirti’s chamber there are many of the Small Vehicle, and at mealtime they see no water in their bowls and no smoke in the stove, and every one of them breeds the weary thought of longing for food. Though I am good at talking of non-duality, I am ashamed to lack Vimalakirti’s spiritual power to send someone to the Fragrant Land to beg a meal and so relieve the hunger of the assembly. Graciously favored with your compassionate thought, you have met again in the Hall of Universal Light; the timber was procured in the south yesterday and has now reached the other shore. The sea of Dharma is boundless, and all depends on your spiritual transport. Words cannot express my joy. I think that if we gain that much again and fill the three thousand worlds, then we may spread the Pure Land three times over and give room to the emanation Buddhas of the ten directions. If a single hair’s tip is lacking, then we must trouble you to snap your fingers again.

Men of old for the most part forgot their bodies for the Dharma, but I had not seen the real thing; now I have seen it in you, sir. Who today does not talk loudly and high-mindedly, while sowing hell-seeds within the Buddha’s gate? Yet when it comes to plucking out a single hair, all is bound up with birth and death; who can be like you, sir, freed in this life, looking on death and life as a game, with every calamity clear to you and the mind unmoved? What the ancients called a man of great strength is just such a one as this. I have heard that a bodhisattva, for the sake of all living beings, gladly endures the suffering of the three evil paths. You, sir, for the sake of the living beings of the great earth, give up this body and life; this is still a small outlay for a great return. I remember the words you spoke when we parted: ’May the old master teach the Dharma and benefit living beings; I take peace and joy in it, and will die for the Dharma-gate.’ That one word entered into this poor monk’s adamantine heart, and through kalpas it will not decay; even when I become a Buddha I cannot forget it. This is not something a man who is not a great bodhisattva could do. Since entering the land of miasma, because of that one word I cannot be idle for a single moment; I make saving living beings my sole business, and the Buddha-Dharma my life. Now I have written, within three years, various books that all reveal the mind-seal of the Buddhas and patriarchs and investigate the purport of the great teachings, and with these I pray for the sage’s longevity without bound and repay a ten-thousandth part of the virtue of one who guards the Dharma. I only pray that you, sir, leaning on this Dharma-power, may soon receive liberation, and that in whatever years remain you may do boundless Buddha-work.
Reply to Gong Xiuwu

Tracing out the three questions you asked, all come from this mountain monk’s single phrase, ’no-thought.’ Yet unless your own earnest practice at your original ground had reached this point, your inquiry could not have come to such a pitch. Men today who practice mostly fall into the trap of the knowing mind and mistake the threshold of light and shadow, taking mere clear numinous awareness as wondrous awakening, not knowing that this clear numinous awareness is precisely glittering idle thought. And then they use the mind to await awakening, thinking there really is a scene there, a place to be attained. All such men have not reached the ultimate source of mind; with a thinking mind they measure a state beyond thinking. But when this mountain monk speaks of no-thought as empty, it is not the annihilation of knowing nothing, the empty emptiness of the glib. The treatise says: the essence of mind is beyond thought; the mark of being beyond thought is equal to the realm of space. For our mind-essence is itself numinous, clear and utterly penetrating, vast, empty and still; it has originally not a hair of idle thought or feeling, is pure and luminous, utterly without a single dharma, forever beyond all views, and originally without the marks of body, mind and world. But a single deluded view is the root of birth and death; how much more so all manner of calculation and reckoning. In practice the first thing is to believe with certainty that one’s own mind is originally pure, luminous and vast, and to observe that this present body, mind and world are all illusory and unreal, like things in a dream, like floating clouds in the sky, suddenly arising and suddenly ceasing. Their arising and ceasing is their own; our mind-essence is still and extinct, clear and unmoving. Though there be all manner of discriminating and reckoning thoughts, they are always idle thought, for in the pure mind there is originally no such thing. Because the mind is originally unborn, this mountain monk speaks of no-thought. What is absent, then, is only all discriminating and deluded thought; how could it be annihilation, dull and without knowing? Therefore old Pang said: only wish to empty what there is; never fill what there is not. Thus this mountain monk, showing men how to practice, first has them believe firmly in their own minds; then in all times they should simply observe spontaneously. Whenever a thought arises, it is idle thought: fix your gaze on it once and for all, and examine where after all this thought arises from. If you do not know where it arises, do not say you have no doubt; when doubt reaches its extreme, you will know of yourself. But not knowing is also no license to calculate, nor may you continue to climb after conditions. Looked at thus, with long familiarity it becomes pure, and the mind-essence is naturally numinous, clear and still; all idle thoughts and feelings before you dissolve like ice in hot water, and at the very thought are transformed into the true mind. Only then will you believe your own mind to be truly so vast, numinous, clear and still, and begin to believe that mind, Buddha and living beings are originally equal, clear beyond doubt, with no other thought remaining. If indeed there is no other thought, then think thought after thought; what after all is thought? At this point there is no scene to be had either: this very thing is practice, and there is no need to seek another master. Yet in this practice you must never use the mind to await awakening, nor take the threshold of light and shadow for a real thing, nor keep the ancients’ words in your breast and take them for your own knowledge and views, nor turn them into an intellectual mystery, nor remove what is before you to seek a better place elsewhere. Mind and conditions are originally one suchness; you cannot split them into two, nor say that the mind sits in the breast in utter darkness, which the ancients called the black mountain ghost. If you fall into that, it is hardest of all to get out. If the mind-essence is beyond thought, that is the land of eternal stillness and light; why seek another Pure Land? If a single thought is perfect and clear and the mind-essence is beyond thought, then wherever you touch you meet the source, and you may be called a man of great freedom. If you truly believe this saying of mine, then your three former doubts are cut off at once, and there is no need to weigh and split hairs. To search out and arrange everything one by one only adds to the idle thought of seeking. Since you are earnest in the Way, I only pray that from now on you put down all your former cleverness and knowledge and views, and put down as well all seeking for the mysterious and the wondrous, all Buddhist knowledge and views. When all holy and ordinary feelings are exhausted, what is it if not the real? This is what is meant by: only exhaust ordinary feeling; there is no other holy understanding.
The Dream-Wandering Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Fifteen
To Lu Wutai, Grand Minister

I bow before the old benefactor, who personally received the Vulture Peak entrustment and came into this final Dharma, manifesting the body of an official to uphold the teaching of the semblance age. For several decades the Dharma-gate has hung by a single thread on the nine tripods, and you alone, old benefactor, have shouldered it. When this mountain monk dwells alone in the mountains and forests, he is ever moved by the deep grace of one who guards the Dharma, and never fails to weep with tears running down his cheeks. Formerly I counted it a lack that I had not been able to pay my respects; when we met briefly at Jetavana in spring, I already rejoiced for a lifetime. Afterward, returning east to the sea, I again heard that an icchantika had made a great obstacle to the Dharma, and my heart was much alarmed. Through you, old benefactor, covering me with your robe, not only was the Dharma-gate set at peace, but the great canon was made manifest, and gods and men were no longer alarmed or doubtful. Whenever I face the Three Jewels, this mountain monk burns incense and scorches his arm to repay the mind of Dharma-giving. Boundless thanks. As for the matter of the great canon at Mount Tai, I suppose it has already reached the unrivalled keeper of the canon, Zang; I have not yet heard, but I think his mind of upholding it grows firmer still.
To Li Kuoan, Grand Censor

I remember a moonlit night in Chang’an when we sat knee to knee and spoke heart to heart, and a fine time at the Fragrant Accumulation when we ate our fill of non-duality. Looking back on the dust of the world, we have been cut off from each other ever since; it is several decades now since we parted. I think of your loyal heart and your bond in the Way, steady and bright, ever aloft in the high clouds and the Milky Way. Alas, alas for this turbid world, where the Way goes against the times; living beings of thin blessing cannot behold the auspiciousness of the lin and the phoenix. Without you, elder, it is exactly as when the black dragon loses the pearl beneath its chin: not only is the ninefold abyss lightless, but the poor and the helpless are left unaided; how then can one hope to reach the Land of Bliss and enjoy the abundance of the four requisites? Moreover the hordes of Mara run wild and the yaksas come out on every side to devour the flesh of living men; truly there is no safety, as in a burning house, and not only in the blazing continents and red earth. I bow before you, elder: gather your spirit in calm detachment, ply your blade in the dark void, draw in the clear breeze of pines and bamboo, and send forth the lofty tone of ice and frost, no less than in the ancient age of Fuxi. This mountain monk, through heavy karma and grave fault, has fallen into this sea of miasma, holding on to a single breath, and so four years have passed. Northern snow and the burning south hang ten thousand miles apart; recalling our old roamings, how could they be had again? Yet though this be the farthest frontier and the remote waste, plants and trees have knowing; how could I for a single day forget the kindly grace of spring? I wonder whether in your white-ray light a single ray has ever fallen on this karma-stained ascetic, walking the Buddha-way by the conditions of karma.
Reply to Xu Jianhu, Embroidered-Uniform Guard

You have deigned to ask me several points of Dharma. This dull-rooted, ordinary fellow of mine, how could he match your high expectations? Let me exhaust my small measure of inference and so answer your purport. As for what you call the meaning of the coming from the west: after all, what meaning did the coming from the west have? If the meaning truly came from the west, then before the patriarch came, did the people of this land all lack the Buddha-nature? You should know that this meaning is complete in every person from the first, lacking not a hair, like a bright pearl in the hem of a garment, one’s own from the beginning; the Buddhas and patriarchs only point it out, and originally have no real dharma to give anyone. If you take it as a real dharma, you are far, far off. As for what you call sitting in meditation: Chan does not belong to sitting either. If sitting were Chan, then what are walking, standing and lying down? You should know that Chan is another name for mind. If you understand that the mind-essence is still and extinct, originally unmoving, how could walking or sitting constrain it? If you do not penetrate your own mind, then even sitting is a leftover dharma. Concentration too is not something to enter; if it could be entered, it would not be the great concentration. It is said that the naga is always in concentration, and there is no time when he is not in it; how then could there be entering and leaving? The mind is originally without marks; if there are marks, it is not the true mind. All these are idle thoughts and shadowy things that climb after conditions; how could they be taken for real? As for what you call Buddha-recitation: it is the recitation of one’s own mind. If the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; if mind and land are pure, there is no birth and death and no coming or going. As for what you call looking into the phrase being able to enter the Way: if the Way belonged to the phrase, everyone could enter it easily; yet there are those who look and do not enter. You should know that this was only the one-time expedient of the ancients, like a tile used to knock at a door, or what is called borrowing the road to pass through. How could it be a real dharma? Yet to draw in beginners, one must squeeze through here before one can begin the work of practice. The ancients had their own expedients; they simply took the single holding up of one thought as the main thing. It is like a precious sword held across the sky: Buddha and Mara alike are cut off, and how would the dust of feeling dare come near? Practicing thus, if a single thought is pure and undivided, all conditions fall away at once; this is what is called entering deeply through one gate, and in time you will come to believe in it yourself.
To Kong Yuanzhi

I think how you and I share the same native place; and is that only to share this same turbid land of the five defilements? Traced to its source, our home truly comes from the same one-Dharma pure land. This wild monk knows the way home, and yet must bear to leave you behind; how could he not wish to walk arm in arm with you? Yesterday, on the point of setting out, I wrote a few words and charged Bisheng to leave them with you as a farewell, quoting Wang Wei’s line, ’If you would know how to end old age and sickness, there is only the study of the unborn.’ This is to jab the awl into a literary man’s tender spot. If you cannot awaken and enter here, then I pray you take refuge before the Three Jewels, receive and uphold a scroll of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, recite it carefully until it is familiar, and not forget a single character. When you see me three years from now, let this be your offering. I hear that your companions in the Way have pure faith; I pray you teach them the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, the one gate of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, into which they may enter deeply. I take it your high selection is at hand; when the matter comes, I pray you take good care of yourself. And in this evil world of the five turbidities, unless one embodies the bodhisattva’s great compassion, one can never make living beings rejoice. I pray you embody this.
To Guo Meiming, Grand Scribe

At your command I have written the stupa inscription for Master Mian, and have already sent you my rough draft. I have merely drawn a gourd after its pattern, not daring to add or subtract at will. But as for those few phrases of yours about grieving for one who saw the sorrow of the Dharma-gate, these drip the bitterness of your own heart and liver; yet for Master Mian there was no other way to speak of it. Only at that time I could not help sighing with tears. I have made a point of bringing it out and setting it forth, so that later readers may also be moved by the mind you have today. Will you also count me as one who slanders by adding? As for the inscription itself, it turns the case over cleanly; in that matter I cannot yield to you.
To Wu, Transport Commissioner

You have shown me the letters of famous gentlemen and asked this mountain monk to certify them. For the most part, worldly men who study the Buddha-Dharma are muddled and imprecise, and hard to pin down by marks or settle by a judgment of right and wrong. Unless one has long set his heart on the Buddha-Dharma and the Zen Way, and has successively consulted true teachers to wash away the dregs and scour off the dust of habit, but instead takes only the vague and approximate, learning semblances of phrases to furnish talk, and makes himself a shadow-body of straw, he will by no means glimpse the reality. And even one who truly takes birth and death as the great matter, if he clings to the view of self and sets up walls and moats, is likewise beside the point. There are many so-called famous gentlemen today; how would a wild man beyond the clouds dare rashly rank their merits? Fortunately there is the Dharma-eye of the layman Guan Dongming. Dongming first studied under Master Chutong; reading this letter, in which he strives to save Master Chu from his fault without shrinking from the axe, this is precisely what is meant by not yielding to one’s teacher where benevolence is at stake; none but one furnished with the right Dharma-eye and wielding the sword of wisdom, one fit to be called a bold and mighty man, could do it. I have glanced through it and already see its main purport. Yet Master Guan’s seeing of the nature is not granted to me as thoroughly transparent. In the main, he upholds the teaching and practices it, with bitter care and deep thought, every word having its source, every matter its lord; it is by no means idle talk. Still, from this alone I cannot see Master Guan’s strong point either. If you, sir, would set your heart on this Dharma, then read the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment ten million times, fusing every character into your mind-ground, until words are forgotten and you meet it in accord; then you will of yourself find the place where a single thought tallies. At that hour you will see clearly for yourself, and need not seek the Buddha-Dharma far and wide, nor raise many knowledge and views; surely you will not turn with the heels of other men. An old saying goes: “A true man has his own ambition to pierce the sky; he does not walk where others have walked.” This is no idle talk. If you truly set your course toward this matter, then in earnest take the great matter of birth and death as the one thing to grip tightly, and never make of it a toy to add to the faults of your mouth. Because you meet the Three Jewels with a true heart, this mountain monk too lays bare his heart and liver and shrinks not from censure, speaking thus for your sake.
To Huang Ziguang

From time to time I sit at ease within the light of the ocean-seal, and with the assembly of illusory beings I wave my fly-whisk and converse in silence. A while ago your esteemed brothers appeared blazingly in my samadhi. Dwelling in seclusion far from the market, shutting the door to investigate the mind, with mountain colors before the eyes and the sound of the stream filling the ears, surely you face the Dharma-body and hear its long tongue. Since spring your movements and repose surpass the ordinary, and I know you advance in this Way; my joy is boundless. You also say that something glimmers within that is hard to speak of to worldly men. Truly so is this matter: it lies only in knowing and believing it for oneself, exactly like a mute tasting sweetness or drinking bitterness; how could it really be spoken out? I send you Dahui’s Recorded Sayings; I pray you peel it open from time to time. I hope you will walk arm in arm with this old man, until Buddha and patriarchs yield their seats by thirty days. The watery-moon practice-ground and empty-flower Buddha-work that I have been doing lately show their traces as they come; when the adornments are in order, I shall welcome your staff and shoes and ascend the Dharma-hall together. My right arm has long been numb, so I cannot write a public letter for all; let this one word speak to everyone.
To Huang Wushan

You alone have planted the spiritual root in former lives, though its ripening is not yet deep. What sustains you is the firmness of your faith, which the hordes of affliction and Mara cannot shake. Just now, when you have set down your burden of suffering and should spur on and press forward first, driving ten thousand miles at a stride and mounting this ford and bridge, I never thought that Heaven would shatter the Dharma-banner and that in one morning all would fall apart and scatter, coming to this. To the eye of Dharma this old decayed one sees not a trace of dust; the real grief is for our comrades in the Way, whose strength in the Way is weak and who have lost this support; it is for them that I grieve and long. Decayed as I am, I make benefiting living beings my whole business; if I forget those of your kind, I forget my own vows. This word is no idle one. This journey of ten thousand miles, and the words with which I took leave of each of you, mutually illumine one another; I pray you read them together.
To Huang Baishan

Our Buddha’s appearing in the world depends entirely on the depth of the capacity and the conditions of response, whereby the Dharma’s length or brevity is made manifest. Where the response is deep, it dwells long; where the conditions are shallow, it easily perishes. This is so by nature. Now the ocean-seal practice-ground in the east is like the sun and moon shining into a dark valley: tall pines and huge boulders and dense gloomy thickets keep it from being seen all day long. Seeing now that it cannot dwell long, it is hardly that the Buddha’s light does not shine deeply enough; the real cause lies in those whose capacity answers it, whose afflictions are a dense thicket and whose screening is not shallow. How then can one judge its flourishing or ruin, its staying or going, by ordinary feeling? My wish is that the screening be cleared away at once; what fear then that the light of wisdom will not shine clear? This journey of mine is ten thousand miles of empty sky; the same wind and the same moon: what marks of coming and going are there? Only may your honored father be well and Ziguang be settled; that is enough to set the mind at ease. Some other day, when response and resonance meet, it will be the ocean-seal samadhi as before.
To Jiang Wuyu

When a good teacher appears in the world, he roams at ease like a great lion; all that he does is done as the Tathagata’s envoy, teaching and maturing all living beings, and this he makes his business. Even for the sake of one living being he does not avoid the sharp suffering of the three evil paths, knife-mountains and fire-masses, counting them no affliction. Judged by this old decayed one’s business today, if I could gain but one person who would not retreat from the bodhi-mind and would accomplish the highest bond, then I would be wholly content; otherwise, adornment with the seven treasures is all karma with outflows, and what use is it? Now this old decayed one has cast his body into the realm of Mara for a full twelve years, yet many have opened faith and come to know that there is such a Way; only their conditions are not yet ripe. Compared with the eastern backwater of former days, this is as different as another age. Of those who have followed me at one time or another, you alone had the heaviest habitual defilement; yet now I see your letter, and you have turned over and changed your plan. This is not to fail your own mind. Though ten thousand miles apart, it is as if face to face; how could I not gladly set out on the road?
To the Elders of Jimo

The feelings of parting and meeting, of sorrow and joy from of old; the thoughts of going and coming that wear one out even in dreams. The heart suffers on account of those who know us, and our thoughts are urgent toward those with whom we have affinity; even the sages and worthies of old were so, how much more ordinary men. I have heard that a single drink and a single bite all belong to former conditions, and that in one man’s honor and another’s disgrace the true friendship is seen. As for this wild monk’s dealings with you gentlemen: the joy of twelve years was no less than the love of flesh and blood, and a sending-off of ten thousand miles renewed the sorrow of parting from brothers. Does this not deserve to be called a friendship of a thousand years, an affinity of many lives? The proverb says: to gain the glory of one generation is not so good as to gain the name of one generation. As for this wild monk’s dealings with these mountains and seas, I certainly cannot leave a fragrant memory; at most I give cause for laughter, and I do not know whether children will tell of it and fathers and sons pass it down for several hundred years. How much more to spread the cloud of compassion in a border land, to make the sun of Buddha shine in thick darkness, to open the source of the sea of nature and turn the axis of the loom of letters, to plant the seeds of buddhahood and nurture the embryo of sagehood. This wild monk’s heart knows this public case, and deeply trusts that in what Heaven bears there is something soundless and odorless. Why then dispute the withering of empty flowers, or measure gain and loss with a cataract-clouded eye? If one knows to reject the one and take the other, then you gentlemen may be called friends who have gone beyond the world.
To the Eldest Son of Grand Minister Lu

Your honored father rode the power of compassionate vows, manifested the body of an official, did great Buddha-work, and was the eyes of gods and men for a generation; the worldly and the world-transcending Dharma he beat into one piece and returned altogether to the adamantine mind-ground. This I know well from long acquaintance: from the time he appeared in the world until the final moment when he let go his hand, he never for a single thought abandoned the mind that guards the Dharma or the work of saving living beings. Though he now follows the world in impermanence and goes with illusion and transformation, his Dharma-body is firm; even were the three calamities to spread over all, it would remain clear and ever-abiding. Not only are the merits of the altars of state a blessing for a billion ages; the merit of the Dharma-gate shall stand equal with Mount Sumeru. Alas, the Dharma-banner is broken: on what shall the four assemblies rely? Great benefactor, to whom the white ox-cart was promised, who will grant it now? The sorrow lies in the Dharma-gate, and truly it breaks one’s heart. Happily the layman is a son who can uphold the house, continuing not only the hereditary line but also the fair name of a family that has left the world. The sorrow is there, the joy is here. From this distant wilderness where I lie bound by my guilt, I regret only that I cannot hold a stick of incense and go to the niche-chamber to chant praises of his merit; yet this single thought has already flown beyond the emerald sea and the long sky. Holding up half a verse from afar to offer before the truth, I think that in the still light he must joyfully receive it. May the layman remember this fragment of my heart, and lead a servant to walk three times around beneath his seat on my behalf; let him not reject it as absurd.
To Wang Zhongjia

I remember how in former days I roamed with you and your elder brother while I was still a child. We have been parted for more than thirty years, and I do not know where the days and months have gone. Lately the karma-wind has blown this poor monk down into the land of rakshasa demons; yesterday, coming south to Zhenzhou, we met quite by chance, as in a dream. Seen with feeling, one cannot but grieve; seen with the eye of Dharma, there is not the least coming or going, movement or stillness. This poor monk sits in this land of miasma, where a single breath lasts a thousand days; had I in former years cultivated the Way like this, I need not have yielded to the ancients. Now I mean to wash away all my former faults, and I dare not but spur myself with all my strength; therefore amid carrying the spear I have striven at this mind, and only now do I know that my former knowledge and views mostly fell at the threshold of light and shadow. Had I not received the sage’s grace and the great wielding of the tongs and hammer, how would I know there could be such a day as this? Looking back at the emperor’s claws and fangs, they are no more perilous than Huangbo’s staff; I am ashamed that my dull faculties are not the equal of Linji’s, who at that moment dealt three blows and received one slap.
To Guan Dongming, Assistant Censor

I remember how we once sat facing each other in a mountain tower and I listened to your profound discourse. At that time I was still in my dull ignorance; though I did not know the secrets of Vimalakirti’s chamber, I knew in my heart that you were a man of the inconceivable. Thirty years since we parted, and it seems like a single meal. Truly the Tathagata’s appearing in the world is from beginning to end no departure from the samadhi of the instant. This poor monk often reproves himself: he has lived in this world to no purpose and entered the gate of emptiness in vain. Though he has the will to equal the ancients, he regrets he never had the teachers of old, such as Linji, Deshan and Yunmen, to serve as his models and patterns; so even with the fire of prajna to smelt the gold of the Buddha-nature, to seek to become a true Buddha-patriarch face would surely be hard. Therefore for more than twenty years I have dwelt bitterly in the mountains, and in that midst have not dared lightly let slip a single thread. All manner of illusory conditions are altogether Buddha-work in the void, and I would not let empty flowers cloud my eyes. This single thread of solitary light is known and seen in full only by the Tathagata’s spiritual power and heavenly eye; it can be spoken of only to one who knows me. Lately, by the compassionate pity of the Buddhas’ spiritual power, I have been gathered in by an inconceivable matter. When this worldly calamity first fell on me, I rejoiced in secret, saying that the heavy gates of the Iron Enclosure could not be shattered without such tongs and hammer. Ever since the trials began, I have looked on them only with the adamantine right eye; from first to last the joy within me has been no less than before, and indeed exceeds it more each day. Therefore I am the more grateful for the sage’s compassion and deeply indebted to the Buddha’s power; this mind too is known only to the Buddha. This poor monk has often said that past and present are different ages, sages and ordinary men different roads; yet though their settings differ and their deeds and practices are distinct, each has his own aspiration, and none fails to declare his aspiration through words and to reveal his mind through deeds. The Changes was expounded at Youli, the Li Sao broke forth by the riverbank, the Daodejing was written as he passed the frontier, the Nanhua was composed in reclusion. Though their natures and feelings took different roads, their aspirations were one; all made the mind speak through words and the will appear through deeds. As for this poor monk, I know that my habitual tendencies gather around loyalty and righteousness. I have often thought privately: a true man living in the world, if he cannot uphold the moral order and fulfill human relations, is fortunate at least to wear the monk’s robe, and so should be a loyal minister to the Dharma-king and a filial son to the compassionate father. Therefore for thirty years I have striven bitterly at this matter; even in a cold cliff a thousand feet high, in ten thousand years of ice and snow, piercing bone and heart, dying once and reviving nine times, and that was not only today’s affair. What I regret is that the habitual tendencies of kalpas cannot be exhausted in one lifetime; that is surely hard. Yet I know that of wondrous awakening I dare by no means compare myself with the ancients; but this single thought of pure truth will not retreat through kalpas. This is no idle word. I grieve to think that I was born into this final Dharma, this thin and fading age, and that blown by the karma-wind, busybodies marked me out by a few words as one of the Dharma-gate. I am ashamed that my principle is not full and my practice not complete, so that I cannot win the trust of the world and of later ages. And then I met this adverse condition and fell into the common lot; since my traces are slight, my mind grows ever smaller, and it is the harder to be trusted in one’s own time. As for the great matter of birth and death, it truly rests on oneself; to repay the Buddha’s deep kindness, how could there be no ground? I have heard that a son’s service to his parents is called filial when he does not disgrace his person. Now this poor monk has cut his hair and marred his form, and so cannot be a filial son in the world; and having fallen into guilt and disgrace, he is not equal to finishing the work of leaving the world. Truly he has lost both monk and layman. Has he not lived this life in vain? In truth I wished, at this season when the nine tripods hang by a thread, with the heart of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu, to uphold the life-line of the Buddhas and patriarchs, so as not to fail in being a loyal minister to the Dharma-king. Therefore, even in the midst of the beating, when I was flung into this land of pestilence, I did not dare for a single breath forget the work of saving living beings. Within a few days of entering the land of miasma I took the Lankavatara as my Buddha-work; within three years I have written various books with my own hand, and amid spears and battlements I did not dare be idle for a single breath. The reason I long to settle this public case quickly is this: I think that having long dwelt on the northern frontier and traveled to the farthest south, and having experienced every extreme of heat and cold in the world, how should this tiny body bear such burning and boiling? The will waits while the form already wastes; the day may be long but the life is short. If I do not strive and hold on to this one breath, taking the Dharma as my life, I fear that once I am thrown into a ditch, I shall wither with the grass and trees. And having once lost the human body, it is hard to regain it through ten thousand kalpas; if conditions lead me on another road, and I change face and head, then wishing to use today’s body to do today’s work, to hold today’s words and seek to verify them with today’s teacher, how could that be had again? Therefore I know no shame and do not reckon whether it is fitting, but simply let conditions take their course. If a single word accords with the mind of the Buddhas and patriarchs and wins the appreciation of one who understands the sound, then to die that evening would be enough; what leisure have I to mind the critics, to weigh gain and loss and fit the arguments of men’s mouths? You who know me, sir, will you not count me wild? I have heard that only a sage can penetrate the aspirations of all under heaven and suit the feelings of the multitude; I have not heard that all under heaven can penetrate a sage’s aspiration or that the multitude can suit a sage’s feeling. It rests only within the heart and borrows nothing from outside. Reading your teaching over carefully, I find its praise excessive and beyond the truth; I am deeply moved by the care of your mind that guards the Dharma, grieving with one body. I dare not measure it by common truth. Yet since I have received your honored compassion, the hopes you place on this inferior one are exactly like a mute eating coptis: hard to bring out before others.
